narrative:
The model predicted a 75% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also worked against you; you finished in the third decile compared with an average around the sixth decile for admitted students. These two early indicators of how you performed relative to your classmates carried more weight than any other information the model considered.

Your LSAT score of 38 was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. This score sits slightly above the average of accepted students and therefore nudged the prediction modestly toward passing. Unfortunately, that positive signal was not large enough to offset the two weaker class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 (versus an accepted average of 3.23), lower-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in law school so that your class rank improves significantly by the end of the first year. Retaking the LSAT to boost your score even further could also help. Once you have stronger evidence of consistent high performance, reapply; the model will then see a very different picture.
